name: DoorDash
tagline: DoorDash mastered urgency-driven behavioral design — turning food delivery from an occasional convenience into a daily habit through countdown timers, default tips, and subscription lock-in.
key_insight: DoorDash's behavioral design reveals a fundamental tension in on-demand platforms: the features that make the user experience feel urgent and seamless (countdown timers, pre-selected tips, one-tap reorder) are the same features that obscure true costs and reduce deliberative decision-making. DoorDash charges a delivery fee, a service fee, a small order fee, and applies dynamic pricing — but the total only appears at checkout, after the user has invested time browsing menus and customizing orders (sunk cost). The DashPass subscription ($9.99/month) transforms occasional delivery into a committed habit by making each marginal order feel 'free.' DoorDash is a masterclass in how to design for habitual, low-friction purchasing — and a cautionary tale about what that means for consumer spending.
top_technique: Delivery Time Countdown as Urgency Commitment
top_evidence: DoorDash processes 2M+ daily orders (Q4 2024). DashPass subscribers order 3x more frequently than non-subscribers. Average order value $35 with $8-12 in fees (Second Measure, 2024). 45% of first-time users convert to repeat within 30 days.

techniques.title: Delivery Time Countdown as Urgency Commitment
techniques.description: DoorDash shows estimated delivery time ('35-45 min') prominently before ordering, then switches to a real-time countdown after order placement. The pre-order estimate creates urgency ('if I order now, I'll eat by 7pm'). The post-order countdown creates a psychological commitment that discourages cancellation — the timer makes it feel like a process is already in motion, even during the restaurant preparation phase. If the delivery is late, users feel the loss more acutely because the countdown set a specific expectation. This framing exploits temporal discounting: the concrete promise of food-in-35-minutes feels more valuable than the abstract savings of cooking.
techniques.evidence: DoorDash processes over 2 million daily orders in the US (Q4 2024 earnings). Second Measure data shows average order frequency increased 20% after DoorDash introduced the live tracking map + countdown timer in 2020. Temporal discounting research (Frederick et al., 2002) shows that concrete, immediate rewards are valued disproportionately over abstract future savings — exactly the psychology that makes '$35 for dinner NOW' beat 'save money by cooking.'

techniques.title: Tip Pre-Selection as Social Norm Anchoring
techniques.description: DoorDash presents tip options (15%, 20%, 25%, Other) with a default pre-selected at 15-20% before the order is confirmed. This design exploits multiple biases simultaneously: anchoring (the pre-selected amount becomes the reference point), social norms (seeing percentage options implies 'everyone tips this much'), and guilt avoidance (selecting 'Other' or $0 requires active effort and feels like a deliberate anti-social choice). The tip screen appears after the user has committed to the order but before final payment — a moment of maximum compliance due to sunk cost.
techniques.evidence: DoorDash reported that pre-selected tip defaults increased average tip amount by 35% compared to a blank tip field (DoorDash Engineering Blog, 2022). Research by Thaler & Sunstein on default effects in retirement savings (401k auto-enrollment) shows the same mechanism: the default option captures 80-90% of decisions. Notably, DoorDash's tip goes to drivers but the platform benefits from higher tips through increased driver supply and reduced base pay subsidies.

techniques.title: DashPass Subscription as Habit Lock-In
techniques.description: DashPass ($9.99/month for $0 delivery fees on orders $12+) transforms DoorDash from an occasional convenience into a committed habit. Once subscribed, each additional order feels 'free' because the delivery fee is already paid — classic sunk cost exploitation. The subscription creates a psychological imperative to order more to 'get your money's worth.' The $12 minimum subtly increases average order value. DashPass converts the ordering decision from 'should I order delivery?' (evaluative) to 'what should I order?' (habitual) — the most profitable behavioral transition for any platform.
techniques.evidence: DashPass subscribers order 3x more frequently and have 2.5x higher lifetime value than non-subscribers (DoorDash Q3 2024 investor presentation). The $9.99/month price point requires ~2 orders per month to break even, but the average subscriber orders 5-6 times. This overuse pattern matches the 'gym membership' phenomenon documented by DellaVigna & Malmendier (2006): consumers systematically overestimate their future usage but the subscription itself drives increased usage.

techniques.title: Fee Decomposition and Dynamic Pricing Opacity
techniques.description: DoorDash decomposes the total cost into multiple small fees (delivery fee, service fee, small order fee, regulatory fees) rather than showing one total. This 'partitioned pricing' strategy exploits a documented bias: consumers underestimate total cost when it's broken into components. Dynamic pricing (surge fees during peak times) is displayed as a temporary condition rather than a permanent price, making users feel they're paying 'the normal price plus a surcharge' rather than 'the actual price.' Menu prices are often higher than in-restaurant prices, but this markup is not explicitly disclosed.
techniques.evidence: Second Measure (2024) analysis shows DoorDash fees average $8-12 per order (23-34% of food cost), but users consistently estimate fees at $5-7 when surveyed. Morwitz et al. (1998) demonstrated that partitioned prices are perceived as 15-20% lower than equivalent combined prices. DoorDash was sued in 2020 over deceptive pricing practices (settled for undisclosed terms). The FTC's 2024 'junk fees' initiative specifically targeted delivery platform fee structures.

strengths: Real-time tracking genuinely reduces delivery anxiety
Restaurant discovery and curation adds real value
DashPass creates clear value for frequent users
weaknesses: Fee decomposition obscures true order cost
Tip pre-selection exploits social pressure at checkout
Dynamic pricing opacity during peak hours
